fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sketch: the CFG derivative parser internal to LambekD

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Feasibility sketch for building the inductive derivative parser inside Lambek^{D} in Agda. The claim: it is definable and provable by combining the regex \delta + soundness on the brzozowski branch with \rhd /lob on the box branch; the one design decision is to put the guard in the datatype, and the one genuine risk is refl-time computation. Signatures below are schematic — proofs are holes, never postulates.

fr:title.text: Datatype: guard as a structural invariant

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Datatype: guard as a structural invariant

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The naive recursion δ c (var X) = δ c (def X) does not pass Agda's termination checker — def X is not a subterm and the keystone short-circuit is semantic. So encode the guard structurally, Greibach-style: a nonterminal is its finite list of guarded clauses ⌈c⌉ ⊗ tail.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
NT : Type -- finite context of nonterminals (e.g. Fin n)
data CFGDesc : Type where ⟨I⟩ ⟨⊥⟩ : CFGDesc -- ε , empty lit : ⟨ Alphabet ⟩ → CFGDesc -- ⌈c⌉ var : NT → CFGDesc -- nonterminal leaf _⊗_ _⊕_ : CFGDesc → CFGDesc → CFGDesc
record Production : Type where -- one nonterminal's productions field nullable : Bool -- is ε accepted? clauses : List (Alphabet × CFGDesc) -- guarded: (leading char , tail)
def : NT → Production -- the grammar = a table of productions
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The invariant "every var occurs behind a consumed terminal" is now unforgeable: a nonterminal reaches you only via a clauses entry, whose head is a literal. Unguarded grammars are not expressible.

fr:title.text: The state space is internal, and Löb runs it without enumerating it

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The state space is internal, and Löb runs it without enumerating it

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Reading w moves A to the iterated residual \delta _w A; the reachable states are these residuals, an internal family. For non-regular A it is not finitely presented (e.g. Dyck's unbounded stack), but that never obstructs a parse: the run is a Löb fixed point visiting only the states along the input, generating each transition \delta _c on demand. There is nothing to enumerate.

One internal caveat on variance. The decomposition above exhibits A as an algebra-shaped fixed point through a free iso. The genuinely-extra coalgebra structure is \mathsf {next} : A \vdash \rhd A (suffix-closure), which is not free (sss-00BD) — via \lhd \dashv \rhd it is equivalently \lhd A \vdash A, "every derivative maps back into A". The run needs neither \mathsf {next} nor any chosen coalgebra as extra data — only \nu and \delta — but the gap is why observing (a \rhd - coalgebra) and building (a Löb fixed point) are distinct internal capabilities, related by \lhd \dashv \rhd rather than equal.

fr:title.text: Open recursion for grammars: the contextual Löb rule

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Open recursion for grammars: the contextual Löb rule

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The closed Löb principle {\mathopen {}\left (\rhd A \vdash A\right )\mathclose {}} \Rightarrow {\mathopen {}\left (\top \vdash A\right )\mathclose {}} for the constructed \rhd builds a global term \top \vdash A. That is enough to define a closed recursive grammar, but not to define a recursive parser in a context — parametrised combinators, threaded accumulators, precedence-indexed families. This note records the open (contextual) form as precise entailments, and pins the exact side condition, sharpening sss-00BD's discovery that \mathsf {next} is coalgebra structure rather than a theorem.

The rule. Internalise closed Löb at the exponential \Gamma \Rightarrow A. From \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \Gamma \Rightarrow A closed Löb gives \top \vdash \Gamma \Rightarrow A, i.e. \Gamma \vdash A. Uncurrying the premise, open guarded recursion is

The recursive call is the delayed \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}}; the hypotheses in \Gamma are available now. At \Gamma = \top it collapses (\top \Rightarrow A \cong A) back to closed Löb \rhd A \vdash A. Note \And is a type former and \vdash the hom, so the premise is the single entailment above — not \Gamma conjoined with a judgement.

The catch: firing the call. To apply \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}} you must first produce \rhd \Gamma and use later-applicativity. That needs \mathsf {next}_\Gamma : \Gamma \vdash \rhd \Gamma , which by sss-00BD is not free: it is exactly an \mathsf {IsCoalgebra}\,\Gamma structure, i.e. a suffix-closed \Gamma . So the whole content of "open" reduces to one condition:

html:blockquote.html:p: Open recursion over a context \Gamma is available iff \Gamma carries \mathsf {next}_\Gamma , i.e. iff \Gamma is suffix-closed (a \rhd -coalgebra).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two sources of the step. The delayed argument the recursive call consumes can arrive two ways.

html:ul.html:li: By \mathsf {next} — when \Gamma is a coalgebra. Constant grammars \Delta S, the unit \top (the canonical \top -coalgebra of sss-00BD), and any \rhd B are suffix-closed, so \mathsf {next} exists on them.

By consumption — the parsing-specific route, needing no \mathsf {next}. If the recursive occurrence sits behind A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} with A positive (A\,\varepsilon = \varnothing : no empty parse), then {\mathopen {}\left (A \otimes X\right )\mathclose {}}\,w depends on X only at proper suffixes of w; hence A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} factors through \rhd , and \mu X.\,\mathrm {base} \oplus A \otimes X is a guarded fixed point. The \otimes pays the step that \mathsf {next} would.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This is the precise form of "guardedness by consuming a token": \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} is the single-character \rhd of sss-00AC, and A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} for positive A is its many-step generalisation.

html:ol.html:li: Kleene iteration. \mathsf {iter}\,A := \mu X.\, I \oplus A \otimes X for positive A. Open in the grammar parameter A, which is substituted and sits inside the guard — no \mathsf {next} needed. Cf. greedy Kleene star.

Left folds (\mathsf {chainl1}). Parse p\,{\mathopen {}\left (\mathit {op}\,p\right )\mathclose {}}^{\ast } threading an accumulator a : \Delta {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {Tree}\right )\mathclose {}}. The accumulator lives in a constant grammar — a coalgebra — so the contextual rule applies with \Gamma = \Delta {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {Tree}\right )\mathclose {}}.

Pratt / precedence climbing. \mathsf {pratt} : \Delta \mathbb {N} \vdash \mathrm {Parser}\,E with \mathsf {pratt}\,p recursing at a fresh level p'. This is exactly the precedence-indexed Löb family of sss-00BZ item 1, \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Pi p.\,\mathrm {Parser}\,E\right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \Pi p.\,\mathrm {Parser}\,E; the context \Delta \mathbb {N} is constant, hence a coalgebra, so \rhd distributes through the \Pi .

Attribute grammars. Inherited attributes flow into the recursive calls — the threaded context \Gamma ; synthesized attributes are the result A. The rule applies exactly when the inherited attribute is suffix-closed, which is automatic for position-independent (constant) attributes. A position-varying inherited attribute — a grammar indexed by the input already consumed — is not a coalgebra; this is precisely the boundary of genuinely context-sensitive parsing.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The dividing line. Substituted parameters, constant threads, and \rhd -guarded self-references are all coalgebras, so essentially every standard combinator is open-recursible without the applicative structure of \rhd . The one thing genuinely ruled out is transporting a position-dependent grammar down into the recursion — an inherited attribute indexed by the consumed prefix — which is where sss-00BD's missing \mathsf {next} actually bites.

Semantically this is nothing new beyond sss-00A8: the same well-founded-on-string-length induction that proves closed Löb relativises to any coalgebra context \Gamma , and that relativisation is the rule above.

fr:title.text: Recap: amazing right adjoint to a single character

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Recap: amazing right adjoint to a single character

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Recall from Grammar/Derivative/Base.agda that for a character c the right Brzozowski derivative is the linear residual D_l\, A\, c \;=\; A \mathbin {\htmlStyle {display:inline-block;transform:rotate(180deg);}{\multimap }} \texttt {"}c\texttt {"}. The "amazing right adjoint" — the further right adjoint, in the sense of the tiny-object story — is given by
with the symmetric variant
when the character sits at the end of a string. These already exist in the codebase as √l c A and √r c A, with √l-app witnessing the counit D_l\, (\sqrt {c}\, A)\, c \vdash A.

The amazing-right-adjoint construction goes through for any tiny object, not only single characters. In the grammar setting strings are tiny: an inhabited string is a finite product of literal grammars under \otimes , and \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes - preserves all colimits, so iterating gives a left adjoint \texttt {String}\, w \otimes - with both adjoints on the right.

Notation. For a non-empty string w, write \sqrt [w]{A} for the right-adjoint indexed over w; concretely \sqrt [w]{A} \;=\; (\texttt {String}\, w \otimes \top ) \Rightarrow (\texttt {String}\, w \otimes A) on the left-handed side, with the obvious right-handed dual. The single-character √l c A is the special case w = [c].

Define \rhd A \;:=\; \mathchoice {\textstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\sqrt [w]{A}. A point of ▷ A is a coherent family: for every non-empty string w, a witness that consuming a w-prefix exposes an A. The indexing is by all non-empty strings simultaneously, so the modality is character-agnostic in the same sense as classical guarded type theory's ▷, while being grounded in concrete suffix-extraction at every non-empty depth.
Two design questions are baked into the definition.

html:ul.html:li: Side. We pick the left-handed \sqrt [w]{}, which encodes "any proper suffix"; the right-handed choice gives "any proper prefix". They are symmetric and either could serve. A genuinely two-sided ▷ encoding "any proper substring" is the natural next target — see TODOs below.

Why non-empty. Empty w would give \sqrt [\epsilon ]{A} \cong A, collapsing \rhd A \vdash A into a strict identity and killing Löb. Restricting to non-empty strings keeps the modality genuinely "later".

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The candidate is only useful if it has the structural rules of a later modality. Three properties to check.

html:ol.html:li: Next. A canonical map \mathsf {next} : A \vdash \rhd A. Heuristic construction: for each non-empty w the component should factor through the strength of \sqrt [w]{} on A, packaging the universal property of the amazing right adjoint with the splitting \texttt {String}\, w \otimes \top \vdash \texttt {String}\, w \otimes A that already holds when A is global.

Functoriality and \sqrt {}-applicativity. Since ▷ is a \And -indexed limit of right adjoints it is automatically a right adjoint, hence preserves limits. The genuinely calculus-specific check is the interaction with \otimes : do we get \rhd (A \otimes B) \vdash \rhd A \otimes \rhd B, or its dual, in a way that lets later-style applicative bookkeeping go through?

Löb induction. (\rhd A \vdash A) \;\Rightarrow \; (\top \vdash A). Conjectural argument sketch: from \rhd A \vdash A and next build \rhd A \vdash \rhd A as a \sqrt [w]{}-coalgebra in each component; uniqueness on each component forces the global fixed point, and the limit of "the unique fixed point" is the unique fixed point of the limit. The character-by-character flavor of this matches the well-founded-on-string-length argument used in sss-00A8 to build the Brzozowski parser, suggesting that Löb here is in fact the same principle, repackaged.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two prior trees frame ▷ differently.

html:ul.html:li: sss-00AC treats ▶ either as a primitive guard on μ, or as a single-character alias \rhd _c\, A := A \mathbin {\htmlStyle {display:inline-block;transform:rotate(180deg);}{\multimap }} \texttt {"}c\texttt {"}. The proposal here is closer to the second reading, but quantifies over all non-empty depths at once via an indexed product of amazing right adjoints rather than fixing a single character.

sss-00A7 identifies - \mathbin {\htmlStyle {display:inline-block;transform:rotate(180deg);}{\multimap }} \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} with the Brzozowski derivative; the candidate here is one amazing-right-adjoint level beyond, and the indexing brings in strings rather than single characters.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Atkey's reduct as a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra stack

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Synthesis tying Atkey's data types with negation and the GL-reduct route to complement grammars to the recursive-coalgebra framework of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] that underwrites the derivative-based CFG parser plan and Cass's claim that (\mu F)^{-1} is always recursive.

The Cass–Urbat–Wißmann picture: an intrinsically correct algorithm is the unique c2a-morphism from a recursive coalgebra (C, \gamma : C \to FC) to an algebra (A, \alpha : FA \to A). For a parser, the algebra is \mu F^+ and the coalgebra is the input string with derivative structure. Parse is intrinsically correct because it is unique. This is a purely positive story.
Atkey's reduct is the bilateral generalisation. The doubled fixed point
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: D \;=\; \mu ^i Y.\;{\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\;\nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: forces a \mu on the positive side and a \nu on the negative side. The two sides have dual recursion principles, which already exist in the literature as the two halves of Capretta–Uustalu– Vene:

html:ul.html:li: Positive. Initial algebra \mu F^+; recursion principle is recursive coalgebra (CUV 2006). Style: catamorphism / fold / well-founded. Computes a parse tree.
Negative. Terminal coalgebra \nu F^-; recursion principle is corecursive algebra (CUV 2009). Style: anamorphism / unfold / productive. Computes a refutation trace.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the reduct is a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra bialgebraic construction, doubly nested: an outer \mu ^i in \mathbf {Chu}^i parameterising an inner \mu on the positive side and an inner \nu on the negative side. Each layer has a known universal property. None of this is new — what is new is that putting them together gives complement grammars under recursion.
Cass's claim: the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, regardless of whether it is the final coalgebra. Apply it twice in the reduct stack:

html:ul.html:li: Inner positive. D^+ = \mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-) (with Y^- fixed) is an initial algebra. Its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow structural recursion on parse trees works without step-indexing or guarded modalities.

Outer \mu ^i. The outer fixed point is an initial algebra in \mathbf {Chu}^i. By the same lemma — lifted to \mathbf {Chu}^i, which needs a separate check — its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow recursion on the stage of knowledge Y is well-founded.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dually, the standard CUV theorem the inverse of a terminal coalgebra is a corecursive algebra fires on the negative side, giving productivity for refutation generation. So the negative half also avoids guarded modalities, again contingent on the lemma transporting to our setting.

fr:title.text: Resolution: next is structure, not a theorem

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Resolution: next is structure, not a theorem

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The diagram chase does not go through for arbitrary grammars — the verification check anticipated above fails. next is not derivable from the indexed-product definition of ▷ alone; it requires extra structure on A.

Max's framing. Presheaves on (\texttt {String}, \text {suffix-order}) are precisely \Box -coalgebras over families. The map next : A ⊢ ▷ A is the coalgebra structure, not a global term. So instead of postulating it (or holding it open as a hole), package it as a record:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: record IsCoalgebra (A : Grammar ℓA) : Type ℓA where field next : A ⊢ ▷ A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The canonical example is ⊤-IsCoalgebra: ⊤ is suffix-closed because any suffix of a ⊤-parse is a ⊤-parse. This lives in Grammar/Later/Coalgebra.agda on the guarded branch of gsa-brzozowski.

Löb (sss-00BE) goes through unchanged: the obstruction to next does not block Löb, because Löb is proven directly by well-founded recursion on string length and never invokes a global next.

This is the same shape of design discovery as Cass's recursive-coalgebra framework: well-foundedness + recursion lives on coalgebra structures, not on bare grammars. The connection is made explicit in the recursive-coalgebra synthesis — next is the coalgebra structure that feeds a c2a-morphism.

fr:title.text: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. See also well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek and derivative-based CFG parser via recursive coalgebras.

Cass's suggestion. For an initial F-algebra D, there is an evident subterm ordering on D. The inverse of the initial algebra is a coalgebra structure on D, and it might be possible to show that this coalgebra is well-founded with respect to that subterm ordering — obtaining a recursive-coalgebra witness without going through the final coalgebra.

Stronger claim to check. Cass further suggested that the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, even when it is not the final coalgebra. The approach rests on this claim, and it needs to be verified — dig into the coalgebra literature (Adámek, Capretta, Uustalu, Vene) for the precise statement.

Why this matters. If true, it gives a categorical justification for recursive definitions on initial algebras like the Dyck grammar without invoking step-indexing or guarded modalities. It would complement — or replace — the guarded-modality candidates as the well-foundedness mechanism.
